definition: In regression analysis, least squares is a method to determine the best-fit model by minimizing the sum of the squared residuals—the differences between observed values and the values predicted by the model.
details: Least squares problems fall into two categories: linear or ordinary least squares and nonlinear least squares, depending on whether or not the model functions are linear in all unknowns. The linear least-squares problem occurs in statistical regression analysis; it has a closed-form solution. The nonlinear problem is usually solved by iterative refinement; at each iteration the system is approximated by a linear one, and thus the core calculation is similar in both cases. Polynomial least squares describes the variance in a prediction of the dependent variable as a function of the independent variable and the deviations from the fitted curve. When the observations come from an exponential family with identity as its natural sufficient statistics and mild-conditions are satisfied (e.g. for normal, exponential, Poisson and binomial distributions), standardized least-squares estimates and maximum-likelihood estimates are identical. The method of least squares can also be derived as a method of moments estimator.

explainer.lead: Least squares finds the best-fit model by minimizing the sum of squared differences between observed and predicted values. It matters as the standard fitting method underlying much of regression analysis.

tiers.eli5: It is like drawing the line that sits closest to a scatter of dots, counting how far off it is at each dot and keeping the line with the smallest total error.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers fit linear models in closed form and solve nonlinear models by iterative refinement, approximating the system as linear at each step. A pitfall is that squaring residuals makes the fit sensitive to outliers.
tiers.paperLevel: The method minimizes the sum of squared residuals, the differences between observed values and model predictions. Problems are linear (ordinary least squares, with a closed-form solution) or nonlinear (usually solved by iterative refinement, linearizing at each iteration); the least-squares method for error is attributed to Carl Friedrich Gauss.

explainer.example: Fitting a straight line to measured points by choosing the slope and intercept that minimize the total squared vertical distance from the points to the line.
